body.text: Ozempic-like drugs have exploded in popularity in recent years, with about 500,000 Australians using injectable glucagon-like peptide-1 (GLP-1) receptor agonists each month.
With GLP-1 pills now entering the Australian market, the number of people using this class of medications may soon increase.

Priya Sumithran, head of the obesity and metabolic medicine group at Monash University which has received funding from GLP-1 manufacturers, anticipated some people already using GLP-1 injections would switch to the pill, and others would consider using the drugs for the first time.
"There will be people who were really put off by the fact that it was only available as an injection that might be more interested in considering a treatment if it is not an injection," she said.
GLP-1 drugs can help with weight regulation and chronic health conditions such as diabetes, but there is still a lot we do not know about their use over the long term or by younger patients.
While research continues to probe the real-world impact of GLP-1s, here is what we know so far about potential side effects.
What are GLP-1s?

GLP-1s drugs such as tirzepatide (brand name Mounjaro) and semaglutide (sold as Ozempic and Wegovy) mimic a hormone called glucagon-like peptide-1 to help regulate blood sugar and reduce food cravings.
Although we are hearing more about them now, they aren't an entirely new class of drugs; US regulators approved the first GLP-1 drug to treat type 2 diabetes more than 20 years ago.
More recently, Australia's medicines regulator approved two new daily GLP-1 pills: oral semaglutide (sold as Wegovy) and orforglipron (sold as Foundayo).

Mark Mellor, chair of the Royal Australian College of General Practitioners' obesity management group, said it had been challenging to develop an oral GLP-1 pill because stomach acid and enzymes broke them down.
Research shows people appear to lose more weight using injectable weight loss drugs in comparison to tablets, but more data is needed.
What are the common side effects?
The most commonly reported side effects for the GLP-1 drugs approved for use in Australia are gastrointestinal symptoms such as:
• nausea
• vomiting
• diarrhoea
• constipation
• loss of appetite; and
• bloating.
"These are mostly mild and most commonly happen when you start the medication or when you increase the dose," Dr Sumithran said.

Louise Baur, professor of paediatrics and child health at the University of Sydney which has received funding from GLP-1 manufacturers, said it was important potential side effects of the medications were explained clearly, especially to adolescents and their families.
Professor Baur said most research on GLP-1s to date looked at adults, which meant young people using the drugs should be monitored closely.
"We want people to realise that this is a potentially very long-term medication,"
she said.
What are the less-common side effects?
Patients using weight-loss drugs may face an increased risk of regurgitation or aspiration under anaesthetic.

They may also be at increased risk of developing gallstones, where pebble-like deposits of digestive fluid form inside the gall bladder (although losing weight quickly through any method increases this risk).
The medications have also been linked to a very rare risk of developing pancreatitis, a dangerous inflammation of the pancreas that can be fatal.
But Dr Sumithran said there was "mixed evidence" about this association.
"If it is increased, it's a very, very tiny increase,"
she said.
GLP-1 drugs have also been linked to a rare but serious eye disorder called non-arteritic anterior ischemic optic neuropathy (NAION), which can lead to sudden, painless vision loss.
"People taking these medications should contact their doctor straight away if they've got any of those symptoms," Dr Sumithran said.
What about muscle mass and bone density?
The use of GLP-1 drugs is associated with the loss of muscle mass and a decrease in bone density, although these are linked with rapid weight loss, not necessarily caused by the drug itself.
Dr Sumithran said with all types of weight loss, muscle loss was "inevitable".
As people using these medications had a decreased appetite, she said it was important they prioritised eating nutritious food with lots of protein.
"Exercise is also really important to preserve muscle strength and function, so particularly resistance exercises and strength training to keep your muscles strong," she said.
Research has previously flagged that people using GLP-1s may have an increased risk of micronutrient deficiencies from reduced intake and/or gastrointestinal side effects.
But there's still not enough evidence for this.
Dr Mellor said it was important people using GLP-1s received wrap-around support with continuous monitoring that went "beyond weight loss".
"We need to be thinking about nutrition, physical activity, mental wellbeing, sleep," he said.
He said it was also important clinicians asked about their patients' bone density risk — family history of osteoporosis, for example — and closely monitored those at higher risk.
What happens if you stop GLP-1s?
Some people may discontinue GLP-1 drugs due to side effects or cost.
In Australia, GLP-1 drugs are only subsidised via the government's Pharmaceutical Benefits Scheme (PBS) for type 2 diabetes.
Weekly injections for weight loss cost between $150 and $700 a month, and daily tablets are expected to be between $260 and $400 a month.
"Not everyone is able to afford to use these medications, so it's inevitable that people will stop and start them,"
Dr Sumithran said.

People who stop using GLP-1s typically regain weight within about a month, with most returning to their starting weight within about two years and losing other health benefits such as better blood pressure.
Dr Mellor said anyone thinking about stopping or changing dosages should talk to their doctor.
"Although they have a good safety profile, there are some very serious potential side effects with these treatments," he said.
"These prescriptions need to be provided by practitioners that are skilled in obesity care and understand the risk of these medicines."
